The sequence

Morning reminder

Sets a repeating alarm on weekday mornings, through your phone's calendar.

Add to calendar

A web page can't wake your phone on its own, so this hands the job to your calendar, which can. It repeats Monday to Friday at the time you pick, fires even with the app closed, and you can change or delete it in your calendar like any other event.

Shoes off, socks on the carpet. Nothing here should hurt: a stretch is a broad pull, a pinch is a stop sign. Skip anything your knee objects to.

The six drills

1:30 · Whole joint

Standing hip circles

One hand on the window ledge. Knee to hip height, sweep it out to the side, carry it behind, bring it down. Six seconds a circle, three each direction.

If your torso sways to help, the circle is too big. Shrink it until only the leg moves.

2:30 · Rotation

Floor 90/90

Front leg bent 90° in front, shin across you. Back leg bent 90° out to the side. Hands behind for support, sit tall.

The most valuable drill here. Front hip gets external rotation, back hip gets internal rotation, both in flexion, exactly what cross-legged sitting asks for.

KneesSit up on the edge of an ottoman. Raising your hips takes the strain off both knees and stops your back rounding. Widen past 90° if a knee objects.
No-floor swapSeated wipers on the ottoman, feet wide, both knees dropping left then right.

2:00 · Adductors

Supported butterfly

Back against the sofa base, soles together, heels a forearm's length out. Further away is kinder on the knees and still gets the inner thigh.

Sit tall for a minute, then hinge forward from the hips. Hands rest on your ankles. Never push your knees down.

No-floor swapWide stance, toes pointing straight forward, hands on the ledge. Shift side to side, bending one knee to 45°.

2:00 · Hip flexors

Standing split stance

Back foot a metre behind, back leg straight. Tuck your tailbone and squeeze the back glute before you push forward, then reach the same-side arm overhead.

You sit all day. This is the counterweight, and it stops your pelvis tipping forward and eating your hip flexion.

KneesStanding only. Kneeling and couch-stretch versions are better stretches and worse for your knees.

2:00 · Flexion depth

Knee to ribs

On your back, pull one knee toward the outside of your ribs, toward the armpit, not the chest. Other leg stays flat.

Pulling wide clears the hip socket. A sharp pinch at the front of the hip means back off until it's gone and work just below it.

No-floor swapSit tall on the ottoman and hug one knee to the outside of your ribs.

2:00 · The hinge

Ledge hinge, then hamstrings

Hands on the ledge, walk back until your arms are straight and your torso is horizontal. Push your hips back, let your chest sink.

Then heel on the ottoman, knee soft, hands on your hip bones, hinge with a flat back. Stop the moment your back rounds. That's the range you're training.

Finisher by day

Worth knowing

Why these three things are separate problems

Cross-legged needs external rotation and hip flexion together, plus adductor length. Most people have the rotation and lose it the moment the hip is also flexed.

Toe touch with bent knees is nearly pure hip flexion. Bending the knees rules out your hamstrings: your pelvis isn't rotating over the femurs, so you bend at the spine and run out of room.

Turned-out feet mean the hip sits in external rotation by default and internal rotation has quietly disappeared. That's the direction nobody trains, and the one that matters most for you.

Some of the turnout is bone

The angle of your femoral neck and the orientation of your hip socket are set. Ten to fifteen degrees of turnout per foot is ordinary and always was. At thirty-plus and asymmetric, there's real tissue and habit to reclaim, but no amount of stretching rotates a femur. Measure against your own week-one photo, never against the person in the video.

Range you never load, you lose

Fifteen minutes a day buys you range. Keeping it takes loading it. Two twenty-minute sessions a week (goblet squats to whatever depth your knees allow, split squats, side-lying hip work) and you'll keep roughly three times as much. That's the multiplier, not more stretching.

Consistency beats intensity

Five relaxed sessions beat two heroic ones. On a bad morning switch the session to Short: hip circles, the 90/90, the split stance and the walk, five minutes, and count it done. Saturday and Sunday are rest days by design, and rest is when the tissue adapts. A missed day is nothing. A missed fortnight puts you back to week one.

How this should unfold

Weeks 1-2. Hold everything at four out of ten. Expect to feel like nothing is happening. You're building the habit and letting your nervous system stop guarding.

Weeks 3-4. Move to six out of ten. Retest. Rotation moves before flexion, so the wipers improve before the toe touch. That's the plan working.

Weeks 5-6. Add five minutes at home in the evening: 90/90 and split stance. Frequency beats duration for stiff hips.

Week 7 on. Retest against your week-one photo. Keep this as maintenance and put the effort into loading the new range.

General mobility guidance, not medical advice. Stop anything that produces knee pain. See a physio if pain persists, if you get sharp or catching pain in the hip joint, or if things get worse rather than better over three weeks.

Baseline

Fill these in before your first session, then retest on the Monday of weeks 3, 5 and 7. Hip change is slow enough that you won't perceive it, so these numbers are the only way you'll know it's working. Saved on this device only.

Knees bent 20°, reach down slowly. Where do your fingertips land?

Ankles crossed on the carpet, no forcing. How high is each knee?

Feet wide on the ottoman. How far does each knee drop before the opposite hip lifts?

Stand normally, photograph your feet from above. Don't correct first, and keep the photo.

Date and what changed, each time you retest.
